query: Which specific Afrobarometer items should form a core cohesion index shortlist mapping clearly to inclusive identity, trust, and cooperation, and what is the conceptual justification for each?

response.query: Which specific Afrobarometer items should form a core cohesion index shortlist mapping clearly to inclusive identity, trust, and cooperation, and what is the conceptual justification for each?
response.answer: For a core cohesion index, use Afrobarometer items on trust, inclusive identity, and cooperation for the common good. These items measure social cohesion's three key attributes.

results.title: Conceptualising and Measuring Social Cohesion in Africa: Towards a Perceptions-Based Index | Social Indicators Research | Springer Nature Link
results.content:
Title: Conceptualising and Measuring Social Cohesion in Africa: Towards a Perceptions-Based Index | Social Indicators Research | Springer Nature Link
This paper introduces an innovative method to measure national-level social cohesion based on survey data from 19 African countries. We distinguish three dimensions of social cohesion; i.e. the extent of perceived inequalities, the level of societal trust, and the strength of people’s adherence to their national identity. We develop two social cohesion indices: a national average SCI and a Social Cohesion Index Variance-Adjusted (SCIVA); the latter one takes into account the level of variation across different ethnic groups within countries. We also investigate quantitatively the relationship between countries’ levels of social cohesion and the occurrence of a range of conflict events. As expected, we find that countries with low levels of social cohesion in a particular year according to our SCI are more likely to experience a range of different violent conflict events in the subsequent year. ### Social Cohesion, Politics and Governance in East Africa: Evidence from Afrobarometer Surveys. The use of several items to measure our three dimensions of social cohesion would allow us to reduce measurement errors possible in some of the questions used here: the trust questions could be refined in terms of trust in whom (people from a different ethnicity, religion etc.) and in what situations (e.g. business transactions, private friendships), whereas nationality items could be designed to pick-up intergroup attitudes more precisely: in our country people should be educated in the dominant language; the existence of multiple cultural practices undermines/strengthens our nation etc. This constructed event is a Battle which does not involve a government actor (Codes 2 (rebel force), 3 (political militia), 4 (ethnic militia) in the INTER1 and INTER2 variables). The Riots/Protests event type in ACLED is limited to Riots by only counting cases in which actors were defined as ‘Rioters’ (Code 5 in the INTER1 or INTER2 variables). Events are limited to the Riots/Protest event type to avoid double-counting as Protesters can also be the victim of ‘Violence against civilians’ in the dataset (e.g. in the case of government repression, see above). However, events in which international actors (INTER1 or INTER2 = 8) assist in fighting an internal rebel group is considered as internal conflict (whether or not the government they are assisting is identified in the ALLY categories), e.g. the French military in Mali.

results.title: Concept
results.content: # IDOS' Concept of Social Cohesion. Horizontal dimension (between individuals/groups). Vertical dimension (between individuals or groups and institutions). *“the vertical and the horizontal relations among members of society and the state, which hold society together. Social cohesion is characterized by a set of attitudes and manifestations that includes trust, an inclusive identity, and cooperation for the common good. According to our conceptualization, social cohesion consists of three attributes – cooperation for the common good, trust and an inclusive identity – and does so on two dimensions (figure 1). Focusing on two dimensions within each attribute is important because social cohesion refers to both, the relations between members of society (horizontal dimension) and members of a community and the state (vertical dimension). 1.    **Cooperation for the common good** exists in a society where many people and groups cooperate for "interests that transcend those of the individuals involved".

results.title: AD871: Social cohesion: An African collage of imperfect tolerance and cautious trust – Afrobarometer
results.content: Let the people have a say. Surveys find widespread perceptions of unfair treatment based on people’s economic status. o While intolerance for sexual differences reaches 94% in Uganda, Sierra Leone, and Niger, it is not universal across the continent: Fewer than one-third of respondents express intolerant attitudes toward people in same-sex relationships in Cabo Verde (18%), South Africa (23%), and Seychelles (30%). * Relatives are the only people whom a majority (58%) of Africans say they trust “a lot.” But majorities say they at least “somewhat” trust neighbours, other citizens, people from different religious or ethnic backgrounds, and “other people you know.”. Africans are cautiously trusting: While majorities say they trust other groups of people at least  “somewhat,” only relatives enjoy “a lot” of trust from a majority of respondents, and nearly  half of respondents express little or no trust in people from other ethnic and religious  backgrounds.

results.title: Understanding rapid urbanisation's influence on social cohesion: Insights from Africa - ScienceDirect
results.content: ## Cities. Volume 160, May 2025, 105835. # Understanding rapid urbanisation's influence on social cohesion: Insights from Africa. Author links open overlay panel. Under a Creative Commons license. ## Highlights. This study explores the theoretical channels through which urbanisation affects social cohesion, and then provides empirical evidence. Urbanisation is negatively correlated with the three attributes of social cohesion. Urbanisation-induced changes such as employment, infrastructure, and pollution, are the main channels. The findings underscore the need for inclusive urban development and policies ameliorating social fragmentation from rapid urbanisation. ## Abstract. Africa is currently undergoing the most rapid urbanisation process globally, and this trend is forecast to persist in the coming decades. Many believe that this ongoing rapid urbanisation process is changing the social fabric and reshaping social cohesion. This study explores the theoretical channels through which urbanisation affects social cohesion and provides empirical evidence of their interrelationship. Specifically, the study asks: given the vast social, economic, cultural, political and environmental transformation associated with urbanisation, is there a link between urbanisation and social cohesion? Combining a novel national panel data set on social cohesion from Afrobarometer with urbanisation and other socioeconomic data from world development indicators, the study shows that urbanisation is negatively correlated with the three attributes of social cohesion, namely trust, inclusive identity, and cooperation for the common good. These associations persist even after controlling for country socioeconomic conditions and year fixed effects. Moreover, the magnitude of this association varies across attributes, with trust and inclusive identity showing a higher correlation than cooperation for the common good. Urbanisation-induced change in economic and environmental structure, such as employment, infrastructure, and pollution, are the main channels affecting social cohesion. Overall, the findings underscore the need for inclusive urban development and policies focused on ameliorating social fragmentation resulting from rapid urbanisation unfolding across Africa. ## Keywords. Cooperation for the common good. ## Data availability. Data on social cohesion is publically available from the Afrobarometer website, and data on urbanisation and socioeconomic indicators is publicly available on World Development Indicators website. Night-time light data and other greenhouse gas emission estimates are obtained from Proville et al. Stata codes used are available on request.
